name: Deoxycholic acid (Kybella)

lead: Deoxycholic acid is a bile acid the body makes to digest fat. A synthetic version, sold as Kybella (Belkyra elsewhere), is injected under the chin to destroy fat cells and reduce a double chin, sharpening the jaw and neck line. The FDA approved it in April 2015 for adults with moderate to severe submental fullness.

Injected into fat under the skin, it acts like a detergent that disrupts fat-cell membranes so the cells burst, and the body clears the debris over several months. People discuss it as a lower-downtime alternative to liposuction for the chin and neck, and some ask about other small fat pads; the label does not recommend use outside the chin area, and off-label areas such as jowls and flanks have been tested only in small studies.

paras: It is a clinic procedure done in a series of injection sessions spaced weeks apart. The treated area swells for a period afterward, and the fat reduction becomes visible once swelling settles.

The label lists swelling, bruising, pain, numbness, redness and hardness as the most common reactions. Warnings include injury to the facial nerve branch controlling the lower lip, trouble swallowing and hair loss in the treated area. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Kybella is injected under the chin to destroy fat cells, shrinking submental fullness for a sharper chin-neck line without surgery. The fat reduction shows once swelling settles, and some users ask about other small fat pads, which the label does not cover.

lead: Deoxycholic acid is a secondary bile acid, produced when gut bacteria modify cholic acid, that normally helps emulsify dietary fats [1][2]. A synthetic, injectable form is sold in the United States as Kybella and elsewhere as Belkyra. It is a prescription cytolytic drug that is injected under the skin to destroy fat cells, and it is approved for improving the appearance of moderate to severe convexity or fullness caused by submental fat (a "double chin") in adults [3][1].

The US Food and Drug Administration approved it in April 2015 [1]. The product was developed as ATX-101 by Kythera Biopharmaceuticals [1]. Its label states that it is not approved for subcutaneous fat outside the submental region and that such use is not recommended [3]. Researchers have nonetheless registered or published small studies of off-label areas such as the jowls, upper inner thigh, flanks and bra-strap region [4][5][6][7].

In looksmaxxing communities it appears mainly as an alternative to liposuction for a recessed-looking jawline or neck, and men on looksmax.org have posted about having it done [8]. The label's reported adverse effects include swelling, bruising, pain, numbness and, less often, injury to the facial nerve branch that moves the lower lip [3].

paras: The only approved use is improvement in the appearance of moderate to severe fullness under the chin in adults [3]. A review of male body contouring lists synthetic deoxycholic acid injections among the invasive options for men, alongside liposuction, jawline fillers and implants [9].

Off-label work reported in the literature includes a small prospective study of jowl fat, studies of upper inner thigh fat, and registered trials for flank fat and bra-strap fat [4][5][6][10][7]. The label says use outside the submental area is not recommended [3].

Beyond appearance, the injection has been registered for study in cutaneous neurofibromas in neurofibromatosis type 1, including one trial comparing it with polidocanol, and in superficial lipoma [11][12][13]. These remain investigational.

The label describes Kybella as a cytolytic drug that, when injected into submental fat, physically disrupts the cell membrane and causes the cell to lyse [3]. The molecule is a detergent-like steroid with both water-attracting and fat-attracting regions, which underlies its natural role in digestion [2]. The destroyed fat cells are cleared by the body over the following months [1].

Deoxycholic acid is also a laboratory detergent used in protein isolation [1]. Naturally occurring deoxycholic acid in the gut has been studied in relation to colon and liver disease, but those findings concern the compound made by gut bacteria and are not studies of the injected cosmetic product.
According to the US label, the most common adverse reactions (reported by more than 20% of trial subjects) are swelling at the injection site, hematoma, pain, numbness, redness and induration [3].

The label's warnings cover injury to the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve, which it advises avoiding by following injection technique; difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), with a caution against use in people who already have it; bleeding and bruising, with caution in people on antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy; and alopecia in the treated area [3]. No adequate trials exist in pregnant women, and animal studies at up to five times the maximum recommended human dose showed no fetal harm [3].

Human studies of the cosmetic product include a prospective study of twelve consecutive patients who received injections along a defined zone above the mandibular border to reduce mild to moderate jowl fat, designed to assess safety and feasibility [4]. A phase I trial examined its use for upper inner thigh fat [5], and ClinicalTrials.gov lists small completed phase 4 studies on flank fat, small fatty deformities, bra-strap fat and combinations with triamcinolone for submental fat [14][6][7][15][16]. A registered long-term follow-up study (201 participants) was designed to assess safety and maintenance of effect over 24 months [17].
The pivotal trials behind the 2015 approval are not summarised in the sources used here, so effect sizes are not reported in this article.

A generic version has been available in the United States since April 2021 [1]. In looksmaxxing forums, a user describing a genetic submental fat pad that he felt spoiled his side profile posted that a clinician he consulted recommended Kybella over liposuction and said many men attend her clinic for double-chin and jaw work [8]. Another thread asked whether Kybella could be used in the nasolabial fold fat pad as an alternative to filler [10]; the label states that use outside the submental region is not recommended [3].
